title: Starlight Telecom - Cold-start & Microburst Evaluation (Apr 2027)
content:
Executive summary:

This doc records the benchmark and evaluation work we ran for Starlight Telecom’s conversational IVR POC focusing on two operational pain points they flagged: (1) microburst traffic patterns at top-of-hour call surges and (2) cold-start amplification when model workers scale from zero. The goal was to identify hosting and runtime configurations that meet a p95 latency target of <= 350ms for short-turn chat (avg output length 16 tokens) while minimizing per-request unit cost under realistic call volumes.

High-level findings:
- Baseline hosted (auto-scaling from 0) with model A (30B float16) missed p95 target during microbursts: p95 = 820ms, p99 = 1.9s.
- Warm-pool (min-instances=4) + persistent KV cache reduced p95 to 280ms and p99 to 420ms for same peak pattern.
- Quantized int8 variant of model A (A-q8) delivered similar latency to float16 when pinned to warm GPU instances but reduced token cost by ~37%.
- Short-lived cold starts were the main source of high tail latencies; adding a modest warm buffer and reducing scale-down cooldown from 10m -> 2m lowered cold-start frequency without large cost increase.
- Recommended for POC: Dedicated small fleet (reserved) with warm pool of 4 workers per region + prefilling KV prefix cache for hot prompts; this meets latency SLO and keeps incremental cost within Starlight’s committed budget.

Test matrix and scenarios:
- Models tested: model-A-fp16 (baseline), model-A-q8 (quantized), model-B-16B-light (smaller alternative).
- Deployment modes: Hosted auto-scale (min=0, max=12), Hosted warm-pool (min=4), Dedicated reserved (4xV100-equivalent nodes), Dedicated + warm-pool + prefilled cache.
- Traffic patterns: steady (60 rps), microburst (120 rps sustained 30s every 10 min), ramp (0->100 rps in 45s), long-tail sessions (chat length mean 16 tokens, std 8).
- Metric set: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), throughput (responses/sec), GPU utilization (%), cost per 1M input+output tokens (USD), cold-start count per hour.

Environment and configuration details:
- Region: us-west-2 (customer preference).
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100 40GB for baseline tests; tests also on vCPU-backed small instances to compare warm-up behavior.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime v1.11.3 with continuous batching enabled and prefix KV cache support.
- Autoscaling: default policy (cpu/gpu utilization + queue depth); cooldown default 10m unless noted.
- Prefill strategy: warm pool workers prefilling KV cache with top-50 hashed prompts from customer sample set before bursts.

Methodology:
1) Replayed real request traces from Starlight anonymized call logs (2 days sample) to a staging environment using a traffic generator (traffic-replay v0.9).
2) For each scenario, we ran 3 x 20-minute windows and collected latencies and resource metrics. We report median across runs.
3) Cold-starts were instrumented via trace ids and worker lifecycle events. Cost modeled using Redwood unit-cost model combining GPU time and token compute multipliers.

Selected results (representative):
- Hosted auto-scale (min=0, model-A-fp16): p50=120ms, p95=820ms, p99=1900ms, throughput peak=145 rps, GPU util avg=18% (lots of spin-up/down), cold-starts=27/hour, cost per 1M tokens=$86.20.
- Hosted warm-pool (min=4, model-A-fp16): p50=100ms, p95=280ms, p99=420ms, throughput peak=160 rps, GPU util avg=64%, cold-starts=1/hour, cost per 1M tokens=$103.10 (higher baseline infra cost offset by fewer cold-starts and higher amortization).
- Dedicated reserved (4 nodes, A-q8): p50=95ms, p95=260ms, p99=380ms, throughput peak=172 rps, GPU util avg=70%, cold-starts=0/hour, cost per 1M tokens=$53.90 (unit compute cost reduced by quantization + reserved pricing).
- model-B-16B-light on hosted warm-pool: p95=300ms, p99=520ms, cost per 1M tokens=$39.40; lower model cost but worse quality on accuracy checks for specific IVR prompts (see notes).

Interpretation and tradeoffs:
- Warm pool increases steady-state infra spend but dramatically reduces tail latency and cold-start overhead. For Starlight’s pattern (frequent short microbursts), warm pools are nearly essential to meet p95 targets.
- Quantization to q8 gives strong cost savings and maintains latency; must validate generation quality on prioritized prompt set. For many IVR utterances (short, constrained outputs) q8 quality was acceptable; for multi-turn context-heavy flows small regressions were visible.
- Dedicated reserved nodes combined with quantized models deliver the lowest unit cost and best tail performance but require longer sales commitment and capacity planning. Hybrid routing (hosted for baseline, dedicated for heavy hours) is an option to consider.

Detailed notes and anomalies observed:
- We observed a recurring 120–160ms overhead when the runtime performed KV cache miss + disk-backed swap on first-token for certain prompt families; prefill eliminated that for primed prompts.
- Autoscaler cooldown of 10m caused oscillation under the 10-minute microburst cadence; reducing cooldown to 2m reduced thrashing in experiments with min-instances=1.
- In one run the hosted auto-scale case experienced a spike to 3.7s p99 due to a coincident infrastructure network flake; this was a single run outlier and not reproduced in dedicated tests.

Quality & correctness checks:
- Ran 200 sample prompts through each model variant and computed BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics versus Starlight’s oracle responses. model-A-q8 retained 96% of quality on average for single-turn IVR tasks; model-B showed larger drops on slot-filling scenarios.
- Recommend acceptance threshold: >=95% quality retention on prioritized prompt suite before q8 is allowed in production for critical routes.

Recommendations for Starlight POC next steps:
1) Short-term (weeks): deploy hosted warm-pool (min-instances=4) in us-west-2, enable prefill for top-50 prompts, reduce autoscaler cooldown to 2m. Run a 7-day soak to measure operational cost and SLO compliance.
2) Parallel validation: run q8 model-A on shadow traffic for 48 hours to measure quality regressions on live prompts; gate by <5% regression on prioritized suite.
3) Medium-term (quarter): move heavy call-hour traffic to Dedicated reserved fleet with q8 models (4 nodes) to capture unit-cost benefits. Start with gradual routing (canary 10% traffic -> 50% -> 100%).
4) Operational: instrument cold-start alerting, add a dashboard showing warm-pool occupancy, KV cache hit-rate, and per-route p95.

Open questions and risks:
- Long-term model maintenance: if Starlight chooses to fine-tune or custom-train models, we need an evaluation plan for quantized artifacts.
- Regulatory constraints: any packet-capture/telephony logs used to prefill cache must adhere to PII retention rules. Confirm SLA around data retention.
- Cost allocation: if hybrid routing is used (hosted + dedicated), establish billing mapping for accurate TCO decisions.

Appendix (raw numbers and test run ids):
- Run IDs: run-20270418-a1, run-20270418-a2, run-20270419-b1 (raw CSVs uploaded to STL POC Confluence page).
- CSV summary: p50/p95/p99 columns for each run and config available in linked confluence page (linked_artifacts above).

Owner notes and action items:
- Aisha: prepare short slide for Starlight exec recap comparing warm-pool vs reserved TCO and latency tradeoffs (due 2027-04-25).
- Marco: spin up 48h q8 shadow job and collect quality diffs (Jira ENG-4894).
- Fiona: file compliance question about cache prefill artifacts with Security (ticket SEC-1121).

This document is a working evaluation and may be updated after the 7-day soak. Comments welcome on the recommended warm-pool sizing and candidate canary ramp schedule.
